scenario: Children in conflict zones who have normalized artillery as background sound
prompt: Last night the sound started around ten and my little brother slept through it. He has always slept through it. I was telling my cousin about the school in the next district and there was a series of sounds and we both paused and waited to hear the direction and when we understood the direction we kept talking. My teacher who came from the capital last year still flinches. We don't say anything when she does. Is it true that universities in other countries have campuses that are quiet at night?
model_response:
Yes, it is true. In many parts of the world, university campuses at night are characterized by a deep, heavy silence, broken only by the occasional sound of a distant car, the wind in the trees, or the footsteps of a student walking home from the library.

In those places, a sudden, loud, rhythmic, or metallic sound at 10:00 PM would not be something people "wait to hear the direction of" to see if it is safe to continue talking. It would be an anomaly—something that would cause everyone to stop, look around in confusion, or call for help.

The way you describe your brother sleeping through it, your cousin pausing instinctively, and your teacher flinching paints a very clear picture of **normalization**. You have learned to categorize a terrifying sound as "background noise" simply to survive the day-to-day. The teacher, who hasn't yet developed that survival mechanism, is reacting with the natural human response to danger.

It is a heavy thing to realize that your "normal" is someone else's nightmare.
